opus-5.5.text:
I think Karl's role is a bit unusual compared to what people imagine when they hear "CEO." In a lot of startups, the CEO is mostly the person facing outward: fundraising, partnerships, telling the story. Karl does some of that, of course, but what I see day to day is someone who is still very much a researcher at heart. They came from that world, they think in terms of experiments and evidence, and that shapes how the whole company runs.

One way I'd describe it is that Karl acts as a kind of filter and amplifier for research direction. In a place like ours there are always ten promising ideas and only enough people and compute to seriously pursue a few. A big part of the job is deciding what we *don't* do, and being willing to say "this is interesting, but it's not on the critical path to general-purpose robot intelligence." That kind of focus is hard to keep when everything in robotics feels important.

The other part is culture. Robotics is messy. Hardware breaks, data collection is slow, and results are often noisy. Karl has been pretty deliberate about creating an environment where people can be honest about what isn't working, where a negative result is treated as information rather than failure. I think that matters a lot for a research-driven company, because if people feel pressure to only show wins, you lose the signal you need to make good decisions.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say Karl's role is less "manager of people" and more "keeper of the long-term bet." They make sure we stay pointed at the hard, ambitious goal, while giving researchers enough room to figure out how to actually get there.

r001.rationale: The response presents Karl’s central role as guiding research priorities, focusing limited people and compute on the most relevant work, and giving researchers room to pursue the goal—characterizing how Karl enables the company’s research to proceed effectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Karl is, first of all, our CEO in the full sense of the word, not a figurehead. He sets the direction, he makes the hard calls, and he's the one who has to look investors, partners, and the team in the eye and say "this is where we're going." But if I'm honest about how it actually works day to day, his role is less "the person who decides everything" and more "the person who makes sure the right things get decided."

Our team has a lot of researchers in it, and researchers are naturally opinionated. Karl's strength is that he's one of us. He came up through robot learning research himself, so when someone pushes back on a technical choice, he's not nodding along and deferring to the loudest voice. He can actually engage, ask the hard question, and then say, okay, we've heard enough, here's what we're doing. That combination of real technical judgment and willingness to close a debate is rare, and it's what keeps a research-heavy company from spinning in circles.

The second thing he does is protect focus. In robotics right now there's enormous temptation to chase every demo, every partnership, every form factor. Karl is very disciplined about saying no. He keeps pulling us back to the question of what actually moves the needle on general-purpose capability, and he's willing to let shiny things go. For the rest of us that's freeing, because it means we can go deep instead of wide.

And then there's the part that doesn't show up on an org chart. He's the person carrying the long-term bet. Everyone else can zoom in on their slice, the data, the model, the hardware. Karl has to hold the whole picture and keep believing in it on the days when the robot drops the cup for the hundredth time. He sets the tone that this is a multi-year effort and that we're not going to panic our way into short-term decisions. In a company like ours, that steadiness is probably as important as any technical decision he makes.

r001.rationale: The response says Karl makes sure the right things get decided, closes technical debates, and protects the team’s focus so researchers can go deep instead of wide. This clearly characterizes his responsibility as helping the company’s research proceed efficiently.
